units.translation: to speak ill of one's neighbors when one is ugly
Pelasgia, a name common to several regions which the Pelasgians inhabited, on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 692.

Thus rightly Hermann for τὰν Πελασγίαν πόλιν [the Pelasgian city], which is in M with an inserted gloss, which verses 912 and 1024 had supplied, where χθόνα [land] and πόλιν τήνδε Πελασγῶν [this city of the Pelasgians] (Argos) is read.
you dishonor this city of Pelasgian men
Pelasgus, king of the Argives, who comes on stage in the Suppliants and himself indicates his name at v. 251
For I am Pelasgus, offspring of earth-born Palaechthon
one part Pelasgus, the other the city gives
Explained by the scholiast through ἔνοικοι [inhabitants] and γείτονες [neighbors].
hawks not far behind the doves
Pleiades, the seven daughters of Atlas received among the stars: which constellation is called either in the singular Πλειάς or in the plural Πλειάδες, on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 1179.

For it poets sometimes said Πελειάδες [Pleiades], as Athenaeus teaches 11 p. 491a, citing verses of Aeschylus (fr. 298), in which they are called ἄπτεροι Πελειάδες [wingless Pleiades] διὰ τὴν πρὸς τοὺς ὄρνεις ὁμωνυμίαν [because of the homonymy with birds], as Athenaeus adds.
because of the homonymy with birds
the all-trembling dove has feared exceedingly
Hesychius noted the word as not read elsewhere.
may someone give a man-slaying axe
The same mentions 2, 196. The codices partly have πέλυτρα [shoe-straps]. More serious corruptions of this word are in three glosses of Hesychius: πελλυταί, πελλύτα, πελλύτεμα.

what Critias calls πόδεια [foot-coverings], whether one should think them felt or wrappings, these Aeschylus calls πέλλυτρα [shoe-straps] in the Phrygians (fr. 255): "they have shoe-straps in well-fitted boots"
he prays for an unbearable fate upon the Pelopids
do not wipe out this seed of the Pelopids
Pelops, son of Tantalus king of Phrygia, grandfather of Agamemnon.
to be, a poetic verb, of which only two tenses, present and imperfect, are in use, foreign to comic and prose writers, on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 710.
Thus I corrected for ἀνδρὸς πέλει [of a man it is].
In both places in M πέλῃ [it may be].
never may you see me, O revered Fates, as the sharer of the bed of Zeus
